nodes.question: What is the central objective of the investigation discussed in the paragraph?
nodes.answer: The central objective is to pinpoint the impacts of trade openness, renewable energy consumption, economic growth, and globalisation on environmental degradation in Somalia using annual data from 1990 to 2019.
nodes.paragraph: While scholarly discourse has extensively investigated the environmental degradation arising from the rapid expansion of trade openness, empirical studies have displayed inconsistent findings 14,22,33 35. To the best of our knowledge, there has been relatively little emphasis on investigating the interdependence between trade openness, renewable energy, economic growth, globalisation, and environmental sustainability in Somalia. Despite Somalia S significant reliance on trade, which forms a large part of its GDP through imports and exports, the impact of trade activities on its sustainable development journey remains a critical research question 19. Empirical studies predict that adopting renewable-energy technology is more feasible in nations with greater Scientific Reports trade openness12,28. In contrast to similar studies, the central objective of this investigation was to pinpoint the impacts of trade openness, renewable energy consumption, economic growth, and globalisation on environmental degradation in Somalia using annual data from 1990 to 2019. Accordingly, the present investigation enhances the existing literature in these unique ways. First, it attempts to evaluate the effects of increased trade openness concurrently, the promotion of renewable energy, globalisation, and economic growth on CO2 emissions in a single framework in Somalia.

nodes.question: What is the legally binding target set by the European Climate Law enacted in June 2021?
nodes.answer: The legally binding target set by the European Climate Law is net zero GHG emissions by 2050.
nodes.paragraph: Notable among such actions is the EuropeanClimate Law, enacted in June 2021, which sets a legally binding target of net zero GHG emissions by 2050 and requires both Member States and EU institutions to take the necessary measures to meet this target. This Law also sets an intermediatetarget for 2030 of reducing GHG emissions in the EU as a whole by 55% (from 1990 levels). The success of these agreements critically hinges on the implementation of effective policies at the national level. In this paper, we focus on a particular countrywithin the EU, namely, Spain, in which the basic pillars of such a strategy are the Climate Change and Energy Transition Law, the National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP) 2021 2030, the National Plan for Adapting to Climate Change (PNACC by its Spanish abbreviation) and the Just Transition Strategy; see Banco de Espa a (2021 ). For example, within the framework of the Law on Climate Change and Energy Transition, proposals have been made for notable changes to patterns of mobility and the creation of low-emission zones in major cities.

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: How have past research findings critiqued the ambitions of U.S. cities regarding emissions reduction?
nodes.answer: Past research has documented that U.S. cities have insufficient emissions reduction targets, raising questions about their climate ambitions.
nodes.paragraph: Conventional practice sees cities focusing on reducing emissions from specific domains under their jurisdictional authority, including transportation, waste management, and municipal facilities. Cities have the power to act on other domains such as land use and development, however they often struggle to coordinate climate action through these tools and decision-makers may lack understanding of the scien - tific connections between policy tools and climate (Tang et al. 2010 ; Bierbaum et al. 2012 ). Given limitations to city powers in many contexts, it is not surprising that past research has questioned the ambitions of U.S. cities, documenting insufficient emissions reduction targets (Boswell et al. 2010 ). Further, research on CAPs globally has found that over half of city CAPs fail to set sufficient decarbonization pledges, and evidence-based climate action planning is not prevalent enough (Aboagye and Sharifi 2023 ). As such, there are growing 1 3 61 Climatic Change (2025) 178:61 concerns about whether U.S. cities can or will meaningfully mitigate climate change at the level demanded by the climate crisis (Deetjan et al. 2018 ; Meerow and Woodruff 2020 ).

nodes.question: What is the main objective of the study discussed in the abstract?
nodes.answer: The main objective of the study is to explore the relationship among CO2 emissions, energy use, and GDP in Russia using annual data from 1970 to 2017.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract The aim of this study is to explore the nexus among CO 2emissions, energy use, and GDP in Russia using annual data ranging from 1970 to 2017. We rst conduct time-seriesanalyses (stationarity, structural breaks, and cointegration tests). Then, we present a newD2C algorithm, and we run a Machine Learning experiment. Comparing the results of thetwo approaches, we conclude that economic growth causes energy use and CO 2emissions. However, the critical analysis underlines how the variance decomposition justi es the quali-tative approach of using economic growth to immediately implement expenses for the use ofalternative energies able to reduce polluting emissions. Finally, robustness checks to validatethe results through a new D2C algorithm are performed. In essence, we demonstrate theexistence of causal links in sub-permanent states among these variables. Keywords CO 2emissions Energy use Economic growth Machine learning D2C algorithm Time-series Russia JEL Classi cation B22 C32 N55 Q43 1 Introduction Economic growth affects the way a country uses energy and in return is likely to increase the rate of carbon dioxide (CO 2) emissions in the atmosphere. It comes as a result of development and increases in industries, which consume more and more energy (Malik & Lan, 2016 ).

( 2020 ) and Economic activity and CO 2emissions in Spain 1381 is analysed by Esteve and Tamarit ( 2012a ,b), Sephton and Mann ( 2013 ), Balaguer and Cantavella ( 2016 ), and Moutinho et al. ( 2017 ), among others. In general, models tting the EKC show very diverse evidence. Alternatively, Fosten ( 2019 ) focuses away from the long-run EKC and analyses the short-to-medium run impact of economic activity on CO 2emissions. In the context of the US, Fosten ( 2019 ) proposes a factor-augmented regression model to repre- sent short-to-medium run relationship between seasonally-adjusted monthly growth r a e so ft o t a IC O 2emissions and economic activity, which is represented by a single factor extracted using Principal Components (PC) from a set of macroeconomic vari-ables. He concludes that emissions are not linked to economic activity in the short-run (one month) but nds strong linkages when looking at cycles uncovered at time- scales of length one to three years.
